HYPOTHESIS (data-grounded natural language):

The gardening pathway shows two qualitatively different "prevalence styles" across habitat types, and the distinguishing context is the degree of human modification of the habitat. In strongly anthropogenic, high-richness habitats (Urban, Croplands, and to a lesser extent Riparian), gardening operates in an absolute-flux style: it contributes the largest raw numbers of non-native plant records of any habitat (45 records in Urban, 35 in Riparian, 29 in Wetlands, 23 in Coastal), but it coexists with — and in Urban (29.8% of records) and Croplands (18.5%) is outnumbered by — a dominant unintentional introduction flux carried by disturbance and trade. In contrast, in natural, low-richness habitats (Broad-leaved forests and Coniferous forests, secondarily Wetlands and Coastal), gardening operates in a conditional-dominance style: very few non-natives establish there at all (Broad-leaved forests: 4 records across 68 plots; Coniferous forests: 8 across 77 plots), yet when any non-native does occur, it is almost always a gardening introduction (100% of records in Broad-leaved forests, 87.5% in Coniferous forests, and >50% in Wetlands 55.8% and Coastal 53.5%), with the unintentional pathway virtually absent (0 records in both forest types). This pattern is consistent with gardening-introduced species being habitat specialists with narrow invaded niches — in the species-level data, gardening species have markedly lower invaded niche breadth (median 0.36 vs 0.87 for unintentional species), occupy fewer plots (median 2 vs 3), and have smaller habitat range (mean 2.0 vs 2.7 habitat types) — so they concentrate where they are planted (gardens, urban and riparian settings, wetland and coastal edges) and spill over into nearby natural forests as nearly the sole non-native source, whereas unintentionally introduced weeds spread broadly across disturbed anthropogenic habitats. As secondary corroborating context, the region-wide importance of the gardening pathway has risen steeply over time (16.8% of introductions before 1500 → 75.2% in 1985–2019), implying that the gardening-dominated signature in natural forests is a growing contemporary phenomenon. In marginal habitats (Rock outcrops: 0 gardening records; Scrublands: 2 records, 2.8% plot occupancy), neither style applies — gardening is essentially absent. This is a hypothesis consistent with the data, not a demonstrated causal mechanism; per-plot counts may represent species records or observations (semantics undocumented), and per-habitat sampling effort is unverifiable.

payload.workflow: 1) Parsed invaded_niche_pathways.csv (632 plots, tab-separated) as core evidence; verified n.gard+n.unint+n.agfo=n.total in all rows; aggregated per the 10 habitat levels: (a) absolute Gardening counts and plots occupied, (b) Gardening share of n.total conditional on n.total>0, (c) per-plot Gardening counts given presence (mean/median/max). 2) Contrasted two prevalence styles explicitly: absolute flux (Urban, Croplands, Riparian) vs conditional dominance (Broad-leaved forests, Coniferous forests, Wetlands, Coastal). 3) Support from invasion_success_pathways.csv: dropped the 4 duplicated=TRUE rows (conflicting intro.pathway; documented), leaving 77 species; compared Gardening vs Unintentional on invaded.niche.breadth, number.of.invaded.plots, habitat.range, mrt; habitat.range was NOT numerically equated with the 10 habitat categories. 4) Temporal context from temporal_trends_contingency_table.csv (Gardening share 16.8%->75.2%) woven in as secondary corroboration only. 5) phylogenetic_tree.txt intentionally unused (no habitat/pathway information). 6) Zero-total plots (441/632) reported as a sensitivity analysis on occupancy, not headline, because per-habitat sampling effort is unverifiable; count-semantics uncertainty (species records vs observations) flagged rather than over-claimed; hypothesis phrased as consistent-with-data, not causal.
